The Timken Museum’s HVAC system was operated during part of the evaluation in a manner consistent with how a typical constant air volume (CAV) system would be run, while for other test periods it was run in a manner consistent with operation of a conventional VAV system. The HEDS energy recovery coil and HVAC optimization software were alternately enabled and disabled for periods of both the CAV and VAV system operation to allow comparisons between different baseline configurations and the optimized HEDS operating modes. Although some system design features of the HEDS AHU unit are different than what would normally be implemented in conventional CAV or VAV systems, the comparisons between these four operating modes (CAV baseline, CAV HEDS, VAV baseline, and VAV HEDS) provide a reasonable estimation of differences in energy use that can be expected between the operation of the different HVAC system configurations. 2.1 Summer Evaluation Period (August-September 2023) Table 1 summarizes the operating modes evaluated during different operating periods for the summer evaluation: Table 1. To quantify the two metrics, we compared the water side thermal power to air side thermal power for VAV mode and to enthalpy change 3 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. for CAV mode as the latter has constant airflow. The normalized air side and water side thermal powers for the CAV and VAV operating modes are shown in Figure 2. Since thermal losses from the coils are expected to be very minimal, these heat transfer values should closely match. We see that the air side thermal power aligns better to the water side in the CAV operating modes, when the air flow rate is constant, compared to the VAV modes when the air flow is frequently adjusted.
